rows.speaker: ابن عامر والباقون
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir opens tāʾ in yā abati throughout the Qurʾan; other readers use kasra.
rows.anchor: بفتح التاء في جميع القرآن

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, and probably Ibn ʿĀmir, pause with hāʾ; the others pause with tāʾ.
rows.anchor: وابن كثير يقف على الهاء ب يا أبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatha may restore the feminine tāʾ of a truncated vocative like yā Ṭalḥa; alternatively it preserves the deleted alif of yā abātā, supported by abundant poetry.
rows.anchor: هذا النحو من الأسماء التي فيها تاء التأنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speakers regularized this frequent form through metathesis and deletion; at pause Ibn Kathīr changes feminine tāʾ to hāʾ.
rows.anchor: فلما كثرت هذه الكلمة في كلامهم هذه الكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At pause, sukūn makes the possessive form behave as if it were not annexed, so tāʾ becomes hāʾ; Sībawayh’s truncated khamsata ʿashar illustrates this.
rows.anchor: وإذا سكنت كانت بمنزلة ما لا يراد فيه الإضافة

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir’s pausal hāʾ fits an unannexed vocative like Ṭalḥa or an annexed form with deleted alif.
rows.anchor: كما أنه لو نادى مثل طلحة وحمزة فوقف

rows.speaker: أحمد
rows.claim: Other readers retain tāʾ because a deleted one-letter possessive suffix is structurally attached like a vowel, unlike an omitted independent word.
rows.anchor: والباقون يقفون بالتاء، وهم يكسرون

rows.speaker: أحمد
rows.claim: A one-letter annexed suffix remains attached in analysis, unlike a second word in khamsata ʿashar or an overt noun after Ṭalḥa.
rows.anchor: من حيث كان حرفا واحدا

rows.speaker: أحمد
rows.claim: The deleted possessive yāʾ is treated as retained, just as its vowel remains audible before the pausal consonant.
rows.anchor: فجعلوا الياء المحذوفة في تقدير الثبات كما جعلوا الحركة كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some pause on feminine tāʾ without replacing it with hāʾ; Abū al-Ḥasan cites poetry for this form.
rows.anchor: يقفون على التاء في الوقف ولا يبدلون منها الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic yā abāt restores the deleted consonant of ab and adds tāʾ, rather than using a regular plural ending.
rows.anchor: رد المحذوف من الأب، وزاد عليها التاء كما تزاد

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh observes that when tanwīn is omitted from ʿAnāt, the tāʾ remains kasra, supporting restoration of the deleted stem.
rows.anchor: من حذف التنوين من نحو:

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، الباقون
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads singular āyah lil-sāʾilīn; the remaining readers use plural āyāt.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير: آية للسائلين واحدة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular treats Joseph’s whole story as one sign, as Jesus and his mother are called one sign; the plural makes each episode a sign.
rows.anchor: وجه الإفراد أنه جعل شأنه كله آية، ويقوي ذلك قوله:

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، الكسائي
rows.claim: These readers use ḍamma on the tanwīn before iqtulū; Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥamza use kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع والكسائي: مبين اقتلوا [يوسف/ 98] بضم التنوين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ḍamma breaks adjacent sukūns by matching the following ḍamma, as in madd and ẓulumāt; the kasra reading follows the usual movement of the first sukūn.
rows.anchor: أن تحريكه يلزم لالتقاء الساكنين وهما التنوين والقاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The 4:66 phrase is a parallel for following a later ḍamma when resolving two adjacent sukūns.
rows.anchor: وكذلك: أن اقتلوا [النساء/ 66].

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: All readers use open mīm, assimilate the first nūn into the second, and indicate the assimilated nūn’s ḍamma by ishām.
rows.anchor: وكلهم قرأ: لا تأمنا [يوسف/ 11]، بفتح الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishām prepares the speech organs for an inaudible ḍamma; the assimilated consonant behaves like a pausal consonant, unlike real rawm which separates geminates.
rows.anchor: إنما تهيئة العضو لإخراج ذلك الصوت به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative Arabic form separates the consonants and briefly conceals rather than extends the vowel; both assimilation and this light pronunciation are possible.
rows.anchor: وهو أن تبين ولا تدغم، ولكنك تخفي الحركة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr’s reported reading has first-person nartaʿ and third-person yalʿab, with the latter jussive; other readers differ in person and endings.
rows.anchor: نرتع بالنون وكسر العين، ويلعب بالياء وجزم الباء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو، ابن عامر؛ نافع؛ عاصم، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir use nūn in both verbs; Nāfiʿ uses yāʾ with kasra in nartaʿ; ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī use yāʾ and jussive endings.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وابن عامر: نرتع ونلعب بالنون فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr’s reading best assigns grazing to older brothers and play to young Joseph; the brothers’ guard promise and Jacob’s wolf fear show Joseph’s vulnerability.
rows.anchor: قراءة ابن كثير: نرتع ويلعب بالياء أحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Play is contrasted with truth and condemned when it trivializes religion; irtiʿāʾ is an iftiʿāl form from raʿaytu, like shawaytu/ishtawaytu.
rows.anchor: فأما الارتعاء: فهو افتعال من رعيت

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: Most listed readers pronounce hamza in al-dhiʾb; al-Kisāʾī reads without it, and reports differ among transmitters from Abū ʿAmr and Nāfiʿ.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر وحمزة: بالهمز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-dhiʾb is originally hamzated; tadhāʾabat describes wind coming from every direction, and softening hamza yields yāʾ as in diyāb.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: الذئب مهموز في الأصل

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: One chain alone reports Nāfiʿ with kasra on tāʾ in qālat ukhruj.
rows.anchor: قال: وروى عبد الله عن أبيه عن عامر عن خارجة عن نافع: وقالت اخرج بكسر التاء

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: The other transmitters from Nāfiʿ read the tāʾ with ḍamma.
rows.anchor: الباقون عن نافع: وقالت اخرج بضم التاء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، أبو عمرو، ابن عامر
rows.claim: These readers open the possessive yāʾ and retain alif in yā bushrāy; Warsh from Nāfiʿ transmits sukūn in yā bushrāy and mathwāy.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر: يا بشراي بفتح الياء وإثبات الألف

rows.speaker: ورش عن نافع
rows.claim: Warsh reports sukūn in the yāʾ of yā bushrāy, mathwāy, maḥyāy, and ʿaṣāy; other Nāfiʿ transmitters vocalize it except in maḥyāy.
rows.anchor: ومحياي [الأنعام/ 162] وعصاي [طه/ 18] بسكون الياء

rows.speaker: عاصم، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: These readers omit possessive yāʾ in yā bushrā; ʿĀṣim opens rāʾ, while Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī use imāla.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم وحمزة والكسائي: يا بشرى بألف بغير ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With possessive yāʾ, alif can be accusative as an annexed vocative or genitive like ghulāmī; the ending follows context rather than two case positions at once.
rows.anchor: من قال: يا بشراي هذا فأضاف إلى الياء التي للمتكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For lā bushrā yawmaʾidh, the ending may be built on fatha or accusative because yawmaʾidh attaches to bushrā and lengthens the negated phrase.
rows.anchor: فأما الوجه الذي يكون فيه في موضع فتحه للبناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treating Bushrā as a man’s proper name requires reliable evidence; its vocative means this is the moment of glad tidings.
rows.anchor: فأما من زعم أن بشرى اسم لرجل منادى فيحتاج إلى ثبات ذلك

rows.speaker: عاصم، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim’s fatha on rāʾ is apt because open emphatic rāʾ can block imāla; imāla by Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī is also acceptable.
rows.anchor: وإمالة حمزة والكسائي إياها حسنة أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects adjacent sukūns by analogy and usage, even where the second consonant is geminated; noncanonical readers also replace alif with yāʾ and assimilate it.
rows.anchor: فكرهوا التقاء الساكنين، مع أن الثاني منهما مدغم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No case vowel need be posited on replacement yāʾ: its conversion already signals kasra, as with dual endings.
rows.anchor: إن الياء لا ينبغي أن تقدر فيها الحركة التي قدرت في غلامي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A pausal yāʾ does not establish a connected-case vowel because pause-only forms disappear in liaison; Abū Isḥāq rejects extending them by analogy.
rows.anchor: فلا يثبت في الوصل ويسقط

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abū al-Ḥasan reports some Medinan readers with kasra on possessive yāʾ and calls it defective.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الحسن: قرأ بعض أهل المدينة بالكسر للياء في الإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed basis is a rare deletion like yā tāfī; it is poor usage and analogy because possessive yāʾ behaves like addressee kāf.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: لا وجه لذلك إلا أن يكون جاء به

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abbas reports Abū ʿAmr leaves yāʾ unvocalized; others vocalize it, and al-Yazīdī reports fatha; the vowel clarifies yāʾ after hamza.
rows.anchor: لا يحرك الياء، الباقون بتحريك الياء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr reads hayta laka with fatha on hāʾ, silent yāʾ, and ḍamma on tāʾ; Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir use kasra hāʾ and fatha tāʾ.
rows.anchor: بفتح الهاء، وتسكين الياء، وضم التاء

rows.speaker: هشام
rows.claim: Hishām transmits hamzated hiʾtu from tahayyaʾtu, “I prepared”; al-Ḥulwānī’s fatha-tāʾ version is called an error.
rows.anchor: وروى هشام بن عامر بإسناده عن ابن عامر: هئت لك من تهيأت لك

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة، أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda glosses hayta laka as “come here”; Abū al-Ḥasan notes dialectal tāʾ vowels but says the invitation with open tāʾ is more established.
rows.anchor: أبو عبيدة: هيت لك أي: هلم لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Derived hayta fulānan comes from the vocative like afaf from aff; forms resembling interjections can generate verbs.
rows.anchor: إذا دعاه، فينبغي أن يكون مأخوذا من قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading of hayta as “I prepared myself for you” conflicts with the dialogue: on that interpretation she would say hayta lī, so the report is mistaken.
rows.anchor: ولو كان على هذه الرواية لقالت له: هيت لي، فالوهم في هذه الرواية ظاهر.

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، أبو عمرو، ابن عامر، نافع
rows.claim: These readers use kasra on lām here; Nāfiʿ also reads mukhliṣan with kasra in Maryam, while other verses differ.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وابن عامر: المخلصين

rows.speaker: عاصم، حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī use fatha on lām in these forms throughout.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم وحمزة والكسائي: المخلصين، ومخلصا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kasra means one who makes worship sincere; fatha can mean one chosen by God. Where dīn is explicit, kasra is fixed because religion is the object of sincerity.
rows.anchor: من كسر اللام من المخلصين* ومخلصا* قوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sincerity means worshipping God without partners; the Zumar wording can mean either I make my religion sincere or it is made sincere for Him.
rows.anchor: لا يشركون في عبادته أحدا، كما قال:

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، الباقون
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr alone uses first-person plural nashāʾ; other readers use third-person singular yashāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وحده: يتبوأ منها حيث نشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With yashāʾ, the subject of “wills” matches the third-person subject of yatabawwaʾ; with nashāʾ, Yusuf’s choice can be attributed to God because God empowers it.
rows.anchor: فيشاء مسند إلى فعل الغائب، كما كان يتبوأ كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, Yusuf’s dwellings may be places of worship or enjoining right, so God wills that he stay there; the following first-person verbs support nashāʾ.
rows.anchor: مواضع نسك وقرب، أو مواضع يقام فيها الحق

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، أبو عمرو، ابن عامر
rows.claim: These readers use tāʾ in fityatihi; ʿĀṣim is transmitted with both tāʾ and nūn.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر: لفتيته بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fityah is a small-number plural, fityān a large-number plural; a few attendants suffice to load the bags, while the plural bags support the larger group.
rows.anchor: الفتية جمع فتى في العدد القليل، والفتيان في الكثير

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abū al-Ḥasan says Arabic normally uses fityān even for small numbers unless three or four are specified.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الحسن: كلام العرب: قل لفتيانك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cave youths were reportedly fewer than ten; awʿiyah may denote many despite its small-number pattern because the expected large pattern is unavailable.
rows.anchor: فزعموا أنهم كانوا أقل من عشرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Large-number patterns are avoided where they entail defective-root vowel changes; thinn as plural of thanī is an isolated exception.
rows.anchor: فإذا فعل ذلك فيما لا إعلال فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A large-number plural is rejected when its pattern would entail vowel changes and metathesis; thinn is an isolated irregularity.
rows.anchor: فأما قولهم: ثن في جمع ثني، فمن الشاذ الذي لم يعد إلى غيره

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، أبو عمرو، عاصم، ابن عامر
rows.claim: These readers use nūn in naktal; Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read yaktal with yāʾ.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم وابن عامر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nūn links to “we provision our family, guard our brother, and gain a camel’s measure”; a report from ʿAbd Allāh likewise reads nūn.
rows.anchor: يدل على النون قوله: ونمير أهلنا ونحفظ أخانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ reading can mean the brother himself will collect his measure, as the brothers collect their own loads.
rows.anchor: ووجه الياء كأنه يكتل هو حمله

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Some Ibn Kathīr transmitters omit hamza in istāʾyasū; other transmissions, including Qunbul’s, have hamza between sīn and yāʾ.
rows.anchor: قال أحمد: روى خلف والهيثم عن عبيد عن شبل عن ابن كثير

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: All readers pronounce the final istīʾasa al-rusul with hamza except the cited Ibn Kathīr report.
rows.anchor: وكلهم قرأ في آخرها: استيأس الرسل [110] إلا ما ذكرت عن ابن كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istīʾasa follows the pattern of ʿajiba/istaʿjaba; another form shifts ʿayn to fāʾ and softens hamza, while the transmitted Ibn Kathīr form preserves yāʾ and hamza.
rows.anchor: يئس واستيأس مثل: عجب واستعجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ-first form is original, as verbal nouns show; iyās instead derives from the verb for giving, not despair.
rows.anchor: وهذا مقلوب من يئس ييأس، وهو الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mustaʾāsā means “asking to be given,” derived from giving; the author distinguishes it from forms for healing and grief.
rows.anchor: وكان الإله هو المستآسا إنما هو مستفعل من العطاء

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abū al-Ḥasan analyzes imām in the cited verse as a pattern like a collective noun.
rows.anchor: [الفرقان/ 74] في قول أبي الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In baʿīdu al-saʾw, a verbal noun for the place longed for functions as an adjective; Abū ʿUbayda glosses afalam yayʾas as “did they not know.”
rows.anchor: بعيد المكان الذي يحن إليه ويهيم بلحاقه به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An law yashāʾ Allāh is lightened anna with an implicit pronoun of the matter; a separating particle licenses the following verb.
rows.anchor: أن لو يشاء الله لهدى الناس جميعا [الرعد/ 31] مخففة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The irregular yīʾas meaning “know” cannot extend to yāʾisa meaning “despair”; irregular forms stay confined to their lexical item.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز في: ييأس، هذا الذي بمعنى العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For despair, yāʾisa/yāʾasu is regular like ʿalima/yaʿlamu; its opposite jahila/yajhalu supports the verbal noun yaʾs.
rows.anchor: على هذا المثال وهو: جهل يجهل جهلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem omits thunder because lightning signals it; similarly garments protecting from heat implies cold, and the pronoun may refer to earlier rejecting peoples.
rows.anchor: فأضمر الرعد ولم يجر له ذكر لدلالة البرق عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is unacceptable to say the messengers thought God had falsified His promise or would fail them; such thoughts cannot be attributed to prophets.
rows.anchor: فقد أتى عظيما لا يجوز أن ينسب مثله إلى الأنبياء

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير عن ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr says messengers despaired of their people believing, while their people thought the messengers had lied; divine aid then came.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن جبير: إن الرسل يئسوا من قومهم أن يؤمنوا

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: The majority use two nūns in fanunajjī; ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir also have a one-nūn form. A reported “assimilation” is rejected because the second nūn is silent.
rows.anchor: هذا غلط في قوله: يدغم، ليس هذا موضعا

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim’s one-nūn fanunajjī is a past verb because the narrative is past and aligns with the following passive verb.
rows.anchor: ووجه قراءة عاصم: فنجي من نشاء أنه أتى به على لفظ الماضي

rows.speaker: أحمد بن موسى
rows.claim: A reported Ḥafṣ form with two nūns and fatha on yāʾ is a transmitter error because no governor licenses that fatha.
rows.anchor: كما قال أحمد بن موسى- من الراوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle an in the prohibition may be causal, explanatory, or extra with an implicit verb of saying.
rows.anchor: أن تكون أن الناصبة للفعل، فيكون المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dh urriyyah can be ittakhadha’s second object; on a tāʾ reading it may instead be a vocative, or apposition to the pronoun or Banī Isrāʾīl.
rows.anchor: فأما قوله: ذرية من حملنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wakīl is singular in form but can denote a group, supporting the object analysis.
rows.anchor: لأنه فعل يتعدى إلى مفعولين

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: The plural li-yasūʾū is read by Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, and Ḥafṣ; other transmissions use singular yāʾ or first-person plural nūn.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو، وحفص عن عاصم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We sent them” is omitted after the second corruption because it appeared earlier and is implied by the conditional.
rows.anchor: فحذف بعثناهم، لأن ذكره قد تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faces are a metonym for people and their expressions; the plural best fits the sending and mosque entry, while singular yāʾ may refer to God or the implied sending.
rows.anchor: وجوهكم على أن الوجوه مفعول به لسؤت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: First-person plural li-nasūʾ also attributes the harm to God although the immediate agents are those roaming the land.
rows.anchor: بالنون كان في المعنى كقول من قدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāʾir in the neck means a person’s deed or fate remains attached to him like a collar or chain.
rows.anchor: لزوم ذلك له وتعلقه به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book in wa-nukhriju lahu kitāban is a direct object; “yulqāhu spread open” is supported by the verse about opened scrolls.
rows.anchor: فالكتاب ينتصب بأنه مفعول به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled verb laqqā is transitive to two objects; passivization makes one the subject and leaves the other as object.
rows.anchor: يلقاه منشورا فيدل عليه قوله

rows.speaker: حمزة، الكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisāʾī’s imāla on qāf is acceptable, as is leaving the vowel unchanged.
rows.anchor: وإمالة حمزة والكسائي القاف حسنة وتركها حسن

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: Readers use light mīm in amarnā except Khārija from Nāfiʿ with long ā; Abū ʿAmr is also reported with doubled mīm and Ibn Kathīr with long ā.
rows.anchor: إنها خفيفة الميم، إلا ما روى خارجة عن نافع

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda glosses amarnā as “made numerous,” citing the expression amira Banū Fulān and Labīd’s poetry.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: (أمرنا) أي: أكثرنا

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus reports that Abū ʿAmr rejects the abundance sense for light amarnā.
rows.anchor: وزعم يونس أن أبا عمرو قال: لا يكون في هذا المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Light amarnā may mean commanded or made numerous; the latter is causative. If Abū ʿAmr rejects abundance, the sense is command followed by disobedience.
rows.anchor: فيمن خفف العين، من أن يكون فعلنا من الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamzated āmarnā means God increased them; the author favors abundance because God orders obedience of all people, not only the affluent.
rows.anchor: من أمر القوم، إذا كثروا، وآمرهم الله، أي:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Made them rulers” is implausible because one town cannot have many rulers at once; the people are destroyed through abundant sin.
rows.anchor: ويقوي حمل أمرنا على النقل من أمر

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، أبو عمرو، عاصم، ابن عامر
rows.claim: These readers use singular yablughanna; Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read dual yablughāni.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير، ونافع، وأبو عمرو، وعاصم وابن عامر: (إما يبلغن عندك) على واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular verb takes aḥaduhumā as subject, with aw kilāhumā coordinated; the pronoun in “one of them” already conveys dual reference.
rows.anchor: الذكر الذي عاد من قوله (أحدهما) يغني عن إثبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Or both” is emphatic rather than required, like “dead, not living.”
rows.anchor: ووجه ذلك أنه على الشيء الذي يذكر على وجه التوكيد

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, and ʿĀṣim use yāʾ in lā yusrif; Ḥamza, Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Kisāʾī use tāʾ.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وعاصم: فلا يسرف بالياء جزما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied subject may be the first killer, clear from context; isrāf can be prohibited even where no moderate middle course exists, as with orphan property.
rows.anchor: أن يكون القاتل الأول فيكون التقدير: فلا يسرف القاتل في القتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The victim is aided through retaliation by a guardian or ruler, deterring the killer and serving the life-preserving purpose of retaliation.
rows.anchor: لأن من قتل مظلوما كان منصورا كأن يقتص له وليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Retaliation belongs to the victim’s claim: if he pardons, the guardian cannot retaliate; compensation may settle the claim, yet the victim remains aided.
rows.anchor: في المقتول: منصور، لأنه قد جاء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير، نافع، أبو عمرو، ابن عامر، عاصم
rows.claim: These readers, with Abū Bakr’s ʿĀṣim transmission, use ḍamma on qāf; Ḥafṣ, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī use kasra.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وعاصم في رواية أبي بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qisṭās and qisṭās are dialect variants like qurṭās and qarṭās; Abū al-Ḥasan says ḍamma is more common.
rows.anchor: القسطاس والقسطاس لغتان، ومثله القرطاس والقرطاس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fair measure and weight are obligatory; censure applies to measurable shortfalls, while unavoidable imprecision is excused if one strives within capacity.
rows.anchor: وأما ما لا يضبط فموضوع عنه، لأنه لم يكلف في ذلك إلا الوسع
